paragraph.text: F14. "My vegan burger came with cheese by mistake, so I might as well eat it"

it's a common situation: you order a vegan burger, or ask for no mayo because the house mayo has egg in it, get home and find it came with cheese, egg mayo or butter. It's too late to send it back. In a one-off mistake like this, the reasoning is largely right: the ingredient has already been made and paid for, the sale was recorded as vegan, and eating it or binning it doesn't change what the restaurant will buy tomorrow. Binning it saves no animal and wastes the rest of the meal too. But the first thing to do is tell the restaurant, because that's the only step that changes anything. If that's not possible, eating it, giving it to someone who isn't vegan or simply not wanting to eat it are all reasonable choices. The limit is that this holds for a one-off mistake, not as a rule: it doesn't cover "I ask for it without and, if it comes with, I eat it", nor does it extend to the cheese on the shelf, whose purchase makes the shop restock. And the dilemma doesn't show inconsistency: veganism seeks to avoid exploitation "as far as is possible and practicable", and someone else's mistake isn't your choice.
F. Edge cases and hypotheticals ·
IND ·
leftovers that would be thrown away are covered in F11; this chapter is about a vegan order that came with an animal ingredient by mistake
1. Formulation

"I ordered a plant-based burger with no mayo, because the house mayo has egg in it. I got home and there it was. I can't send it back. If I bin it, the hen gets nothing out of it, and I'm wasting food. So I might as well eat it."
The animal ingredient has already been made and paid for, and the sale was recorded as a vegan meal.
Eating the burger or binning it doesn't change what the restaurant will make or buy in future.
Binning it also wastes the bun, the plant-based patty and the resources used to make them.
So, in a one-off mistake, eating it is at least as acceptable as binning it.

The premises are generally true for a one-off mistake, and the conclusion follows. The problem arises when the conclusion is stretched into "so any product that's already been made can be consumed", or when the mistake stops being a mistake and becomes a habit.
The argument is
and, in the narrow case,
. It fails when generalized: to what's on the shelf, to what's offered at a party, or to the order that "always comes wrong".

3. Answer for children

Imagine you ordered a sandwich without cheese, because you don't want cows to suffer, and it came with cheese. That was someone else's mistake, not yours. Throwing the sandwich in the bin doesn't help the cow, because the cheese has already been made. What helps is telling the shop it came wrong, so they're more careful next time. After that, you can eat it, give it to someone who eats cheese, or not eat it if you don't want to. What's not OK is ordering without cheese and hoping it comes with cheese.
4. Short answer

In a one-off mistake, you're largely right: the cheese or mayo has already been made and paid for, the sale was recorded as vegan, and binning the burger saves no animal. What changes something is telling the restaurant: ask for a remake or a refund, or leave a review. That records the mistake and shows there are customers who want the vegan option done right. If that's not possible, eating it, giving it to someone who isn't vegan or not eating it are all reasonable choices. Just don't turn the exception into a rule: the cheese at the supermarket has also "already been made", but buying it is what makes the shop restock.
"If binning it doesn't help animals, what does? Telling the restaurant, or letting the mistake slide?"

(b) Where the argument breaks

text.bold: 1. Telling the restaurant is what changes something.

paragraph.text: A complaint records the mistake, may get you a remade meal or a refund, and shows there are customers who want the vegan option done right. Eating it or binning it sends no signal at all to whoever got it wrong.

text.bold: 2. In a one-off mistake, eating it doesn't increase demand.

paragraph.text: The sale went through as a vegan meal. The restaurant won't buy more cheese or more eggs because you ate what came by mistake.

text.bold: 3. Binning it doesn't undo the harm and wastes the rest.

paragraph.text: The cheese or egg has still been produced, and goes in the bin along with the bun, the plant-based patty, and the water, land and work used to make them. According to the FAO, about a third of the food produced in the world is already lost or wasted.

text.bold: 4. Giving it to someone who isn't vegan may be the best option.

paragraph.text: If that person would eat a burger with meat, cheese or egg anyway, they eat this one instead, and nothing is wasted.

text.bold: 5. Not eating it is also reasonable.

paragraph.text: Some people feel disgust, and there's a moral reason to refuse even when the harm is done. Think of a human case: if an ingredient came from a system that exploits people, many would refuse to eat it, even knowing it would change nothing. The refusal isn't about consequences, but about not treating the victim as a product (F11). No one is obliged to eat what they see as the product of exploitation.

text.bold: 6. The limit: it only holds for a one-off mistake.

paragraph.text: If it becomes a habit ("I ask for it without and, if it comes with, I eat it"), the mistake stops being a mistake, and the restaurant loses its reason to get it right. If a place gets it wrong almost every time, ordering there again is already a choice.

text.bold: 7. It doesn't extend to what's on the shelf.

paragraph.text: The cheese at the supermarket and the meat at the butcher's have also "already been made". The difference is that buying them is exactly what makes the shop restock (K1, K2). What makes the mistake acceptable, no effect on demand, is what every ordinary purchase lacks.
Eating a burger with cheese in front of others can give the impression that "vegans eat cheese when they feel like it". Explaining what happened avoids the misunderstanding.

Veganism seeks to avoid exploitation and cruelty "as far as is possible and practicable", and doesn't promise purity (L12). Someone else's mistake isn't your choice. Thinking about what to do next is a sign that a person takes animals seriously, not that veganism is inconsistent.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: then it applies to anything that can't be undone

The most serious version says that if vegans can eat the cheese that came by mistake, because "it can't be undone", then they can eat the egg cake already sitting at the party, the leftover cheese in a colleague's fridge, the pizza someone ordered and no one wants. There's always some animal product that "has already been made". So the criterion would be useless.
(e) Why the reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: The question is whether your choice changes the future.

paragraph.text: In a one-off mistake, it doesn't. At a party, it does: whoever bought the food counts on people eating it and, if vegans eat it, the host buys it again next time.

text.bold: Accepting what's offered teaches the opposite.

paragraph.text: Declining kindly and explaining shows the host what to buy next time (J12). Eating it teaches that it makes no difference.

text.bold: Genuine leftovers are a different case, and already debatable.

paragraph.text: Eating what really would be thrown away, with no one counting on it, is the case in F11, and even there it has limits: recurring leftovers become demand.

text.bold: The criterion separates the cases well.

paragraph.text: It doesn't say "anything already made can be eaten", but "what you eat mustn't make anyone produce more". Most cases that seem "impossible to undo" fail this test.

text.bold: When in doubt, not eating it costs little.

paragraph.text: When it's unclear whether the gesture will create demand, declining rarely harms anyone.

11. What the argument gets right

The argument is right about the one-off mistake. Binning it saves no animal, wastes food, and the blame for the mistake doesn't lie with whoever ordered correctly. Vegans don't need to turn a mistake into a moral crisis.

But the same reasoning doesn't work for what you buy at the supermarket or accept at a party, because there the choice changes what gets produced. The best thing to do is tell the restaurant, decide without guilt what to do with the meal, and not turn the exception into a rule.
